questions.question: Name and place the three subtropical anticyclones that control South Africa's weather, state the direction of circulation around them, and describe the weather character they share.
questions.expected_answer: The South Atlantic High over the ocean west of the country, the South Indian High over the ocean to the east, and the Kalahari High over the interior plateau. In the Southern Hemisphere air circulates anticlockwise around a high. All three consist of subsiding air that warms by compression as it descends, dissolving cloud and producing stable, dry, clear conditions with diverging surface flow.

questions.question: Explain, using the inversion layer, why the interior plateau has dry winters and thunderstorm-rich summers.
questions.expected_answer: Sinking air over the plateau creates an inversion — a layer where temperature rises with height — that acts as a ceiling on rising air. In winter the strong Kalahari High presses the inversion below the level of the escarpment, so moist maritime air cannot climb onto the plateau and rising thermals are capped: the interior stays cloudless, dry and frosty. In summer surface heating weakens the high, the inversion lifts well above the escarpment, and humid air from the South Indian High streams onto the plateau beneath it, feeding almost daily afternoon thunderstorms.

questions.question: Describe the mechanism of the berg wind, including the adiabatic arithmetic, and explain why berg-wind days are the country's most dangerous fire days.
questions.expected_answer: In winter the interior high piles cool dense air onto the plateau about 1 500 m above sea level. When a coastal low or approaching front lowers pressure at the coast, this air drains seaward and descends the escarpment, compressing and warming at about one degree Celsius per hundred metres — roughly fourteen degrees of warming over the descent. It arrives at the coast as a hot, very dry, gusty offshore wind that can push winter coastal temperatures into the mid-thirties. Fire danger peaks because the wind combines heat, extremely low humidity and strong gusts over dry winter vegetation, so any spark spreads rapidly; management includes fire bans, firebreaks, warnings and standby firefighting crews.
